sentences.text: Concavenator was a medium-sized primitive carnosaurian dinosaur that reached lengths of about 6 meters.
This carcharodontosaurian weighed between 320 and 400 kilograms.
Its skull measured 63 centimeters in length.
Unlike most relatives, it possessed tall neural spines on its last dorsal vertebrae that formed a sail-like structure.
The skeleton features a series of small bumps on the ulnas and a small crest over the pelvis.
The fossil preserved integument traces, including scale impressions on the feet and tail.
It possessed structures on its ulna resembling quill knobs, a feature previously known only in birds and feathered theropods.
The well-preserved fossil remains were discovered in 2003 at the Las Hoyas paleontological site in Cuenca province, Spain.
The fossils were found by paleontologists José Luis Sanz, Francisco Ortega, and Fernando Escaso, who named the genus Concavenator in 2010.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as MCCM-LH 6666, was described in 2010 by these researchers in the journal Nature.
The specimen found in Las Hoyas is the most complete articulated dinosaur skeleton ever found in the Iberian Peninsula.
Fossil evidence shows Concavenator had broad rectangular scales on its tail underside, bird-like scutes on its feet, and plantar pads on the soles of its feet.
No skin impressions were found near the arm, though large-scale impressions were preserved elsewhere.
Phylogenetic analyses recovered Concavenator as an early-diverging member of the Carcharodontosauridae family.
Concavenator is more derived than its African ancestor Veterupristisaurus, indicating that Carcharodontosaurids were expanding to Europe by the early Cretaceous.
The type species of the genus Concavenator is Concavenator corcovatus, and the animal is classified within the class Reptilia.
Concavenator corcovatus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically the Barremian stage, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago.
Fossil evidence suggests Concavenator lived in a wetland environment with lakes, ponds, and flooded soils containing aquatic plants, ferns, conifers, and early angiosperms.
The function of Concavenator's back crest is unknown, with hypotheses ranging from visual display to thermal regulation.

The interpretation that the bumps on Concavenator's ulna represent quill knobs remains controversial among experts, with Darren Naish speculating that the nodules are too far apart and irregularly spaced to serve as feather anchors.

Andrea Cau compared Concavenator's forearm to those of Allosaurus and Acrocanthosaurus, showing the specimen's forearm is dislocated and the ulnar bumps are on the anterior surface rather than the posterolateral surface.
Cau concluded that the ulnar bumps likely formed part of a crest on the anterior side of the ulna, possibly for muscle insertion connecting the ulna and radius.
